nodes.name: Proof of the characterization of the selection event
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$ via the frozen-residual recursion for the event; Gaussian regression and norm-direction independence for the second point.
nodes.statement:
{\bf First and third points: } The first point works by induction. The initialization of the proof is given by the second point of Lemma~\ref{lem:FirstKnotLaw}. We will use Proposition~\ref{prop:moulinette} to prove the first point. We have
\begin{align}
&\lambda_{k+1}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}\leq Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}\notag\\
&\Leftrightarrow
\forall j\neq i_1,\ldots, i_{k}\,,\ Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j\leq Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}\notag\\
&\Leftrightarrow
\forall j\neq i_1,\ldots, i_{k}\,,\ Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_j-Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_{i_k}\frac{\tau_{j,i_k}}{\tau_{i_k,i_k}}\leq Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}-Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}\frac{\tau_{j,i_k}}{\tau_{i_k,i_k}}\notag\\
&\Leftrightarrow
\forall j\neq i_1,\ldots, i_{k}\,,\ Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_j\leq Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})} \\
&\Leftrightarrow
\lambda^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_{k}= Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}\notag\,.
\end{align}
using~\eqref{eq:rec_Zj} and that~$1-{\tau_{j,i_k}}/{\tau_{i_k,i_k}}>0$ (which is a consequence of~\eqref{eq:sign_tau} and~\eqref{hyp:IrrAlongThePath})  in~\eqref{eq:rec_sign1}. By induction and using~\eqref{eq:rec_sign1}, it holds that
\begin{align*}
\big\{
&\lambda_{k+1}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}\leq Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}\leq Z_{i_{k-1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-2})}\leq\ldots\leq Z_{i_2}^{(i_1)}\leq Z_{i_1}\big\}\notag\\
&\Leftrightarrow\big\{\forall j\neq i_1,\ldots, i_{k}\,,\ 
Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_j\leq Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}\leq Z_{i_{k-1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-2})}\leq\ldots\leq Z_{i_2}^{(i_1)}\leq Z_{i_1}\big\}\\
&\Leftrightarrow\big\{\forall j\neq i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}\,,\ 
Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_j\leq Z_{i_{k-1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-2})}\leq\ldots\leq Z_{i_2}^{(i_1)}\leq Z_{i_1}\\
&\quad\quad \text{and }\forall j\neq i_1,\ldots, i_{k}\,,\  Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_j\leq Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}
\big\}\\
&\Leftrightarrow\big\{\lambda^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_{k}\leq Z_{i_{k-1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-2})}\leq\ldots\leq Z_{i_2}^{(i_1)}\leq Z_{i_1} \text{ and }\lambda^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_{k}=Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}
\big\}\\
&\ \  \vdots\\
&\Leftrightarrow\big\{\lambda^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{a-1})}_{a}\leq Z_{i_{a-1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{a-2})}\leq\ldots\leq Z_{i_2}^{(i_1)}\leq Z_{i_1}\\
&\quad\quad  \text{ and }\lambda^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_{k}= Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}
\leq\ldots\leq \lambda^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{a-1})}_{a}=Z_{i_a}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{a-1})}
\big\}\tag{$s_a$} \\
&\ \  \vdots\\
&\Leftrightarrow\big\{\widehat \imath_1=i_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k}=i_{k}\big\}\,.
\end{align*}
Now, observe that~$\widehat i_{k+1}$ is the (unique) arg max of~$\lambda_{k+1}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}$ on the event~$\big\{\widehat \imath_1=i_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k}=i_{k}\big\}$. 


\noindent It yields that 
\begin{align*}
\big\{\widehat \imath_1=i_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k+1}=i_{k+1}\big\}=\big\{
\lambda_{k+1}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}=Z_{i_{k+1}}^{(i_1,\cdots, i_{k})}
\leq 
Z_{i_k}^{(i_1,\cdots, i_{k-1})}\leq\cdots\leq 
Z_{i_2}^{(i_1)}\leq
Z_{i_1}\big\}\,,
\end{align*}
as claimed. Stopping at~$a$ as in~\eqref{eq:stopa} gives the second part of the statement. The third point of the proposition is a direct consequence of the first point.

\medskip

\noindent
{\bf Second point: }The proof of the second point can be lead by induction. The initialization of the proof is given by the first point of Lemma~\ref{lem:FirstKnotLaw}. Now, observe that~$Z_{i_{k}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}, \cdots, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, Z_{i_1}$ are measurable functions of~$(Z_{i_1},\ldots,Z_{i_{k}})$ and one may check that~$(Z_{i_1},\ldots,Z_{i_{k}})$ is independent of $(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{k}}$. We deduce that~$Z_{i_{k}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}, \cdots, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, Z_{i_1}$ are independent of~$(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{k}}$. One can also check that~$Z_{i_{k+1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}$ is independent of~$(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{k+1}}$.  Deduce that the variables $Z_{i_{K}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K-1})}, \cdots, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, Z_{i_1}$ are independent and independent of $(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{K}}$. This gives the first part of the second point of the proposition. 

Now observe that $(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{K}}$ is a linear function of $P^\perp_{K}Y$. More precisely, consider the vector $\widetilde W:=(Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{j})_{j\in[p]}$ and note that 
\[
(\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}})^2=\frac{\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|_2^2}{n-K}
\quad\mathrm{and}\quad
\widetilde W=\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top\big(P_K^\perp(Y)\big)\,,
\]
where $\theta^K:=(\theta_{j}(i_1,\ldots, i_K))_{j\in[p]}$, $P_K^\perp=\mathrm{Id}_n-P^{(i_1,\ldots, i_K)}$, and with the convention $0/0=0$. The key remark is that the direction and the norm of a centered Gaussian vector are independent, namely $\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|$ is independent of $P_K^\perp(Y)/\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|$ when $\mathds EP_K^\perp(Y)=0$. Observe that $\mathds EP_K^\perp(Y)=P_K^\perp(X\beta^0)$ and $\mathds EP_K^\perp(Y)=0$ is equivalent to $X\beta^0\in H_K$. We deduce that if $X\beta^0\in H_K$ then $\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$ is independent of $\widetilde W/\sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$, as claimed.

We deduce that if $X\beta^0\in H_K$ then $\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$ is independent of $\widetilde W/\sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$, as claimed.

nodes.name: Induction setup
nodes.statement_short: Induction with base case from the first-knot lemma.
nodes.statement: The proof of the second point can be lead by induction. The initialization of the proof is given by the first point of Lemma~\ref{lem:FirstKnotLaw}.

nodes.name: Independence of frozen knots
nodes.statement_short: Measurability and Gaussian independence propagate to all frozen knots.
nodes.statement:
Now, observe that~$Z_{i_{k}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}, \cdots, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, Z_{i_1}$ are measurable functions of~$(Z_{i_1},\ldots,Z_{i_{k}})$ and one may check that~$(Z_{i_1},\ldots,Z_{i_{k}})$ is independent of $(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j)_{ j
eq i_1, \ldots, i_{k}}$. We deduce that~$Z_{i_{k}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}, \cdots, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, Z_{i_1}$ are independent of~$(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j)_{ j
eq i_1, \ldots, i_{k}}$. One can also check that~$Z_{i_{k+1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}$ is independent of~$(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j)_{ j
eq i_1, \ldots, i_{k+1}}$.  Deduce that the variables $Z_{i_{K}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K-1})}, \cdots, Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}, Z_{i_1}$ are independent and independent of $(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}_j)_{ j
eq i_1, \ldots, i_{K}}$. This gives the first part of the second point of the proposition.

nodes.name: Linear function of residual
nodes.statement_short: Frozen residuals are a linear function of $P_K^\perp Y$.
nodes.statement:
Now observe that $(Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}_j)_{ j\neq i_1, \ldots, i_{K}}$ is a linear function of $P^\perp_{K}Y$. More precisely, consider the vector $\widetilde W:=(Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{j})_{j\in[p]}$ and note that 
\[
(\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}})^2=\frac{\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|_2^2}{n-K}
\quad\mathrm{and}\quad
\widetilde W=\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top\big(P_K^\perp(Y)\big)\,,
\]
where $\theta^K:=(\theta_{j}(i_1,\ldots, i_K))_{j\in[p]}$, $P_K^\perp=\mathrm{Id}_n-P^{(i_1,\ldots, i_K)}$, and with the convention $0/0=0$.

nodes.name: Norm-direction independence
nodes.statement_short: Norm and direction of a centered Gaussian vector are independent.
nodes.statement: The key remark is that the direction and the norm of a centered Gaussian vector are independent, namely $\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|$ is independent of $P_K^\perp(Y)/\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|$ when $\mathds EP_K^\perp(Y)=0$. Observe that $\mathds EP_K^\perp(Y)=P_K^\perp(X\beta^0)$ and $\mathds EP_K^\perp(Y)=0$ is equivalent to $X\beta^0\in H_K$. We deduce that if $X\beta^0\in H_K$ then $\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$ is independent of $\widetilde W/\sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$, as claimed.

nodes.name: Proof of the uniform law of the transformed knots
nodes.statement_short: Restrict the joint density, use centering under the null and admissibility to condition on $\widehat m=a$, then change variables by the CDFs.
nodes.statement:
Fix~$a$ such that~$0\leq a\leq K-1$ and consider any selection procedure~$\widehat m$ satisfying~\eqref{e:stopping_rule}. From Theorem~\ref{thm:Main1} (more precisely~\eqref{zaz0}) we know that the density of~$(\lambda_{a+1},\lambda_{a+2},\ldots,\lambda_K)$ conditional on 
\[
 \mathcal F:=\big\{\widehat \imath_1 =i_1, \ldots, \widehat \imath_{K}=i_{K}, \lambda_a,\lambda_{K+1}\big\}\,
 \]
 is given by 
    \begin{equation}
    \notag
    (const)   \Big(\prod_{k=a+1}^K \varphi_{m_k,v_k^2}(\ell_k)\Big)\, \mathds{1}_{\lambda_a \leq \ell_{a+1}\leq \cdots \leq \ell_K\leq  \lambda_{K+1}}\,.
   \end{equation}
   From Proposition~\ref{prop:H0}, conditional on~$\mathcal F$ and under the null hypothesis described in Proposition \ref{cor:Main1}, we know that~$m_{a+1}=\ldots=m_K=0$. It implies that~$\Phi_k$ is the CDF of~$\lambda_k$ for~$a<k\leq K$. 
 
From the definition of a stopping time given by~\eqref{e:stopping_rule} and on the event~$\mathcal F$, we know that~$\mathds{1}_{\{\widehat m=a\}}$ is a measurable function of~$\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_{a-1}$ which are respectively equal to~$Z_{i_1},\ldots,  Z_{i_{a-1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{a-2})}$ on~$\mathcal F$ by~\eqref{e:frozen} (as proven in Appendix~\ref{app:recursion}  and Eq.~\eqref{e:lambda_max}). By Proposition~\ref{prop:reccur} (more precisely~\eqref{e:indep_sigmas}), we also know that this function is independent of~$(\lambda_{a+1},\lambda_{a+2},\ldots,\lambda_K)$ conditional on~$\mathcal F$. Remark that its is also independent of~$\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$ conditional of~$\mathcal F$ for the same reason (it would be useful later, when we will build testing procedures when the variance is unknown). We deduce that the conditional density above is also the conditional density on the event 
 \[
 \mathcal G:=\big\{\widehat m =a,\widehat \imath_1 =i_1, \ldots, \widehat \imath_{K}=i_{K},\lambda_a,\lambda_{K+1}\big\}\,.
 \]
From~$F_k=\Phi_k(\lambda_k)$ ({\it i.e.,} applying the CDF) we deduce by a change of variables that conditional on the selection event~$ \mathcal G$, the vector~$(F_{a+1},\ldots,F_K)$ is uniformly distributed on 
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{D}_{a+1,K}:=&
\big\{
(f_{a+1},\ldots,f_K)\in\mathds{R}^{K-a}:\ \\
&\mathcal{P}_{a+1,a}(F_{a})\geq f_{a+1}\geq \mathcal{P}_{a+1,a+2}(f_{a+2})

\geq \cdots
\geq \mathcal{P}_{a+1,K}(f_K)\geq \mathcal{P}_{a+1,K+1}(F_{K+1})
\big\}\,,
\end{align*}
where~$\mathcal{P}_{i,j}$ are described in~\eqref{eq:pij}.

nodes.name: Conditional density
nodes.statement_short: Conditional density of the later knots from the joint law.
nodes.statement:
Fix~$a$ such that~$0\leq a\leq K-1$ and consider any selection procedure~$\widehat m$ satisfying~\eqref{e:stopping_rule}. From Theorem~\ref{thm:Main1} (more precisely~\eqref{zaz0}) we know that the density of~$(\lambda_{a+1},\lambda_{a+2},\ldots,\lambda_K)$ conditional on 
\[
 \mathcal F:=\big\{\widehat \imath_1 =i_1, \ldots, \widehat \imath_{K}=i_{K}, \lambda_a,\lambda_{K+1}\big\}\,
 \]
 is given by 
    \begin{equation}
    \notag
    (const)   \Big(\prod_{k=a+1}^K \varphi_{m_k,v_k^2}(\ell_k)\Big)\, \mathds{1}_{\lambda_a \leq \ell_{a+1}\leq \cdots \leq \ell_K\leq  \lambda_{K+1}}\,.
   \end{equation}

nodes.name: Centering under the null
nodes.statement_short: Under the null the means vanish, so $\Phi_k$ is the CDF of $\lambda_k$.
nodes.statement: From Proposition~\ref{prop:H0}, conditional on~$\mathcal F$ and under the null hypothesis described in Proposition \ref{cor:Main1}, we know that~$m_{a+1}=\ldots=m_K=0$. It implies that~$\Phi_k$ is the CDF of~$\lambda_k$ for~$a<k\leq K$.

nodes.name: Condition on model size
nodes.statement_short: Admissibility and independence allow conditioning on $\widehat m=a$.
nodes.statement:
From the definition of a stopping time given by~\eqref{e:stopping_rule} and on the event~$\mathcal F$, we know that~$\mathds{1}_{\{\widehat m=a\}}$ is a measurable function of~$\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_{a-1}$ which are respectively equal to~$Z_{i_1},\ldots,  Z_{i_{a-1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{a-2})}$ on~$\mathcal F$ by~\eqref{e:frozen} (as proven in Appendix~\ref{app:recursion}  and Eq.~\eqref{e:lambda_max}). By Proposition~\ref{prop:reccur} (more precisely~\eqref{e:indep_sigmas}), we also know that this function is independent of~$(\lambda_{a+1},\lambda_{a+2},\ldots,\lambda_K)$ conditional on~$\mathcal F$. Remark that its is also independent of~$\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}$ conditional of~$\mathcal F$ for the same reason (it would be useful later, when we will build testing procedures when the variance is unknown). We deduce that the conditional density above is also the conditional density on the event 
 \[
 \mathcal G:=\big\{\widehat m =a,\widehat \imath_1 =i_1, \ldots, \widehat \imath_{K}=i_{K},\lambda_a,\lambda_{K+1}\big\}\,.
 \]

nodes.name: Change of variables
nodes.statement_short: Change of variables gives the uniform law on the domain.
nodes.statement:
From~$F_k=\Phi_k(\lambda_k)$ ({\it i.e.,} applying the CDF) we deduce by a change of variables that conditional on the selection event~$ \mathcal G$, the vector~$(F_{a+1},\ldots,F_K)$ is uniformly distributed on 
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{D}_{a+1,K}:=&
\big\{
(f_{a+1},\ldots,f_K)\in\mathds{R}^{K-a}:\ \\
&\mathcal{P}_{a+1,a}(F_{a})\geq f_{a+1}\geq \mathcal{P}_{a+1,a+2}(f_{a+2})

\geq \cdots
\geq \mathcal{P}_{a+1,K}(f_K)\geq \mathcal{P}_{a+1,K+1}(F_{K+1})
\big\}\,,
\end{align*}
where~$\mathcal{P}_{i,j}$ are described in~\eqref{eq:pij}.

nodes.name: Proof of the conditional CDF of a knot
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the uniform law, then de-condition since $\mathds F_{abc}$ depends only on $\sigma$, $\lambda_a$, $\lambda_c$ and the middle indices.

nodes.name: Integrate
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the uniform law to get the conditional CDF.

nodes.name: Dependence of F_abc
nodes.statement_short: $\mathds F_{abc}$ depends on few variables.
nodes.statement: Then note that the function~$\mathds{F}_{abc}$ is defined by~$\sigma,\lambda_a,\lambda_c,\widehat \imath_{a+1}, \ldots,\widehat \imath_{c-1}$ only.

nodes.name: De-condition
nodes.statement_short: De-condition on the other variables.
nodes.statement: We deduce that we can de-condition on~$\widehat m =a, \widehat \imath_{1},\ldots,\widehat \imath_{a}, \widehat \imath_{c},\ldots,\widehat \imath_{K}$, which gives the result.

nodes.name: Proof of independence of the knots and the variance estimator
nodes.statement_short: Frozen knots are independent of $\widehat\sigma$; on the selection event they are the knots, and $\widehat\sigma$ is the norm of a truncated Gaussian vector.
nodes.statement:
Let us fix some values~$i_1, \ldots, i_{K+1}$. Recall  that the frozen values of the knots
\begin{equation}
\notag
 \lambda^f_1 : = Z_{i_1}, \ldots , \lambda^f_{K} :=Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_{K-1})}_{i_{K}},\lambda^f_{K+1} :=   Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{i_{K+1}},
  \end{equation}
  are Gaussian, independent, and 
 $
\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}
\protect\mathpalette{\protect\independenT}{\perp} \big(Z_{i_{K+1}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K})}/\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}\big)
\protect\mathpalette{\protect\independenT}{\perp} Z_{i_{K}}^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{K-1})}
\protect\mathpalette{\protect\independenT}{\perp} \cdots 
\protect\mathpalette{\protect\independenT}{\perp} Z_{i_{2}}^{(i_1)}
\protect\mathpalette{\protect\independenT}{\perp} Z_{i_1}
$, see Proposition~\ref{prop:reccur} and~\eqref{e:indep_sigmas}. Let us condition by~$\{\widehat\imath_1=i_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K=i_K, \lambda_{K+1} = \ell_{K+1}\}$. Note that, on this event,~$ \lambda_h^f = \lambda_h$ ,~$h \in [K]$ and by Proposition~\ref{prop:reccur} this event is equivalent  to 
 \begin{equation} \{ Z_{i_1}>\cdots >Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_{K-1})}_{i_{K}}> \max_j Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{j}=\lambda_{K+1} = \ell_{K+1} \}.
\end{equation} 
Because of the independence above, we get the conditional independence stated in the first and second point of the proposition. 

\noindent
For the last point, consider $\widetilde W:=(Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{j})_{j\in[p]}$ and note that 
\[
(\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}})^2=\frac{\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|_2^2}{n-K}
\quad\mathrm{and}\quad
\widetilde W=\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top\big(P_K^\perp(Y)\big)\,,
\]
where $\theta^K:=(\theta_{j}(i_1,\ldots, i_K))_{j\in[p]}$, $P_K^\perp=\mathrm{Id}_n-P^{(i_1,\ldots, i_K)}$, and with the convention $0/0=0$. Now, let $U\in\mathds R^{n\times (n-K)}$ be any matrix such that $UU^\top=P_K^\perp$ and define $W:=U^\top Y/\sigma$, then 
\[
\Big(\frac{\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}}{\sigma}\Big)^2=\frac{\|W\|_2^2}{n-K}
\quad\mathrm{and}\quad
\widetilde W=\sigma\times\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top UW\,.
\]
Because of the independence above and \eqref{e:se_prop}, the distribution of~$\widehat \sigma$ is independent of the other variables and such that 
\[
\Big(\frac{\widehat \sigma}{\sigma}\Big)^2=\frac{\|W\|_2^2}{n-K}\quad\mathrm{with\ }W\mathrm{\ s.t.\ }\|\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top UW\|_\infty=\ell_{K+1}/\sigma\,.
\]
This implies that the conditional distribution is the one claimed.

nodes.name: Recall independence
nodes.statement_short: Recall independence of the frozen knots and $\widehat\sigma$.

nodes.name: Condition on selection
nodes.statement_short: Condition on the selection event characterized by the proposition.
nodes.statement:
Let us condition by~$\{\widehat\imath_1=i_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_K=i_K, \lambda_{K+1} = \ell_{K+1}\}$. Note that, on this event,~$ \lambda_h^f = \lambda_h$ ,~$h \in [K]$ and by Proposition~\ref{prop:reccur} this event is equivalent  to 
 \begin{equation} \{ Z_{i_1}>\cdots >Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_{K-1})}_{i_{K}}> \max_j Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{j}=\lambda_{K+1} = \ell_{K+1} \}.
\end{equation} 
Because of the independence above, we get the conditional independence stated in the first and second point of the proposition.

nodes.name: Equation (7.2)
nodes.statement: \{ Z_{i_1}>\cdots >Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_{K-1})}_{i_{K}}> \max_j Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{j}=\lambda_{K+1} = \ell_{K+1} \}.
nodes.label: e:se_prop

nodes.name: Represent via W
nodes.statement_short: Express $\widehat\sigma$ and the frozen residuals via $W=U^\top Y/\sigma$.
nodes.statement:
For the last point, consider $\widetilde W:=(Z^{(i_1,\ldots i_K)}_{j})_{j\in[p]}$ and note that 
\[
(\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}})^2=\frac{\|P_K^\perp(Y)\|_2^2}{n-K}
\quad\mathrm{and}\quad
\widetilde W=\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top\big(P_K^\perp(Y)\big)\,,
\]
where $\theta^K:=(\theta_{j}(i_1,\ldots, i_K))_{j\in[p]}$, $P_K^\perp=\mathrm{Id}_n-P^{(i_1,\ldots, i_K)}$, and with the convention $0/0=0$. Now, let $U\in\mathds R^{n\times (n-K)}$ be any matrix such that $UU^\top=P_K^\perp$ and define $W:=U^\top Y/\sigma$, then 
\[
\Big(\frac{\widehat \sigma^{i_1,\ldots, i_{K}}}{\sigma}\Big)^2=\frac{\|W\|_2^2}{n-K}
\quad\mathrm{and}\quad
\widetilde W=\sigma\times\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top UW\,.
\]

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement_short: Truncation of $W$ gives the law of $\widehat\sigma$.
nodes.statement:
Because of the independence above and \eqref{e:se_prop}, the distribution of~$\widehat \sigma$ is independent of the other variables and such that 
\[
\Big(\frac{\widehat \sigma}{\sigma}\Big)^2=\frac{\|W\|_2^2}{n-K}\quad\mathrm{with\ }W\mathrm{\ s.t.\ }\|\mathrm{Diag}(\mathds{1}_p-\theta^K)^{-1}\times X^\top UW\|_\infty=\ell_{K+1}/\sigma\,.
\]
This implies that the conditional distribution is the one claimed.

nodes.name: Proof of uniformly most powerful GSt in the orthogonal design
nodes.statement_short: Three monotonicity steps (in $c$, $b$, $a$); each compares rejection regions of equal null mass and uses a measure transport with a coordinate-wise nondecreasing alternative density.
nodes.statement:
Let~$\mathcal I$ the set of admissible indexes 
~$$
 \mathcal I := \{a,b,c: a_0\leq a<b<c \leq K+1 \}\,.
~$$

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width=0.3\textwidth]{fig1.png}

\includegraphics[width=0.3\textwidth]{fig2.png}
\includegraphics[width=0.3\textwidth]{fig3.png}
\caption{Rejection domains associated to the different comparison sets appearing in steps of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:zazPower}.} \end{figure}

 
 \noindent
 {$\circ$ \bf Step 1: } We prove that, when the considered  indexes such that~$c+1\leq K+1$ belong to~$\mathcal I$,~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c+1}$ is more powerful than~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$. Our proof is conditional to~$F_a=f_a,F_{c+1} =f_{c+1}~$.  Note that~$(F_{a+1}, \ldots, F_c)~$ has for distribution the uniform distribution  on the simplex
~$$
  \mathcal S := \{ f_a>F_{a+1} > \cdots > F_c >f_{c+1} \}.
~$$ 
  This implies  by direct calculations that 
~$$
  \mathcal{I}_{ab}(s,t) =\frac{ (s-t) ^{b-a-1}}{(b-a-1)!}
~$$
  and that 
\begin{equation} \frac{   \mathds{F}_{abc}(\lambda_b)   }{\mathds{F}_{abc}(\lambda_a)} = \boldsymbol{F}_{\beta((b-a),(c-b))} \bigg( \frac{ F_b-F_c}{ f_a-F_c} \bigg).
\end{equation}
  where~$\boldsymbol{F}_\beta$ is the cumulative distribution  of the Beta distribution in reference.  Using monotony of this  function the~$\mathcal{S}_{abc}$ test has for rejection region 
  \begin{equation} (F_b-F_c)  \geq z_1 (f_a-F_c) \Leftrightarrow  F_b \geq z_1 f_a +(1-z_1) F_c,
 \end{equation}
  where~$z_1$ is some threshold, depending on~$\alpha$, that belongs to~$(0,1)$. 
  
  
  Similarly~$\mathcal{S}_{ab(c+1)}$ has for rejection region 
  \begin{equation} F_b \geq z_2 (f_a-f_{c+1})  + f_{c+1},
  \end{equation}
  where~$z_2$ is some other threshold belonging to~$(0,1)$. We use the following lemmas.  
 
 \begin{lemma} Let~$c \leq K$.  The density~$h_\mu$ of~$f_1, \ldots, f_c$, conditional on~$F_{c+1}$ with respect of the Lebesgue measure  under the alternative is  coordinate-wise  non-decreasing and given by~\eqref{zazcosh}.
  \end{lemma}
  \begin{proof}
Observe that it suffises to prove the result when~$\sigma=1$. Note that 
~$$
 \lambda_{c+1}^{i_1, \dots, i_c } =   \max_{j\in[p]\,,\   j\neq \overline \imath_1,\ldots,   j \neq  \overline \imath_c}  |Z_j|.
~$$
  Thus its density~$ p_{\mu^0,i_1,\ldots,i_c}$ does not depend  on~$\mu^0_{ \overline i_1},\ldots,\mu^0_{ \overline i_c}$. As a consequence the following variables have the same distribution ;
$ \lambda_{c+1}^{i_1 +\epsilon_1 p, \dots, i_c +\epsilon_c p}~$ , where~$\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_c$ take the value 0 or 1 and  indices are taken modulo~$p$. 



Because of the independence of the different variables, the joint density, under the alternative hypothesis, of $\lambda_1, \ldots,  \lambda_{c+1}$ taken at~$ \ell_1, \ldots, \ell_{c+1},$  on the domain~$ \{\lambda_1>\cdots > \lambda_{c+1}\}$ takes the value
~$$
 (Const)   \sum'   \big(\varphi(\ell_1 -\mu^0_{j_1} ) +\varphi(\ell_1 +\mu^0_{j_1} ) \big),\ldots ,
   \big(\varphi(\ell_c -\mu^0_{j_c} ) +\varphi(\ell_c +\mu^0_{j_c} ) \big)
  p_{\mu^0,j_1,\ldots,j_K}(\ell_{k+1}).
~$$
Here the sum~$ \displaystyle \sum'$ is taken over all different~$j_1, \ldots, j_c$ belonging  to~$\llbracket 1, p\rrbracket$.
 
 Then the density, conditional on~$F_{c+1} = f_{c+1}$,   of
~$ F_1 ,\ldots,F_{c}~$  at~$f_1,\ldots,f_c$  takes the value
~
\begin{equation} \mathrm{(const)}  \sum'  \cosh( \mu_{j_1} f_1)\ldots \cosh( \mu_{j_c} f_c) \mathds{1}_{f_1>\cdots> f_{c}> F_{c+1}},
\end{equation}
 implying  that this density is coordinate-wise  non-decreasing. 
 \end{proof}
 
 \begin{lemma} Let~$\nu_0$  the image  on the plane~$(F_b,F_c)$  on the uniform probability  on~$\mathcal S$: it is the distribution  under the null of~$(F_b,F_c)$. The two rejection regions :~$\mathcal R_1$ associated to 
\eqref{ZAZA:e:r1} and~$\mathcal R_2$ associated to 
\eqref{ZAZA:e:r2} 
have  of course the same probability~$\alpha$ under~$\nu_0$. Let~$\eta_{\mu^0}$ the density w.r.t.~$\nu_0$ of the distribution of~$(F_b,F_c)$ under the alternative. Then~$\eta_{\mu^0}$     is non decreasing coordinate-wise. 
  \end{lemma}
  \begin{proof}  
Integration yields that density of~$\nu_0$ w.r.t. the Lebesgue    measure taken at point~$(f_b,f_c)$  is 
\[
 \frac{  (f_a-f_b)^{b-a-1}   (f_b-f_c)^{c-b-1}  }{(b-a-1)!(c-b-1)!}.
\]
  The density of~$\nu_{\mu^0}$  w.r.t. Lebesgue measure  is 
  \begin{equation} \int _{f_b} ^{f_a} df_{a+1} \ldots   \int _{f_b} ^{f_b-2} df_{a+1}  \int _{f_b} ^{f_b-2} df_{b-1} 
   \int _{f_c} ^{f_b} df_{b+1} \ldots   \int _{f_c} ^{f_{c-2}} df_{c-1}   h_{\mu^0}(f_{a},\ldots ,f_c).
 \end{equation}
  Thus~$\eta_{\mu^0}$ which is the quotient  of these two quantities is just  a mean value  of~$h_{\mu^0}$ on the domain  of integration~$\mathcal D_{f_b,f_c}$  in~\eqref{ZAZA:e:vm}.
  
  Suppose that~$f_b$ and~$ f_c$  increase, then all the borns of the domain~$\mathcal D_{f_b,f_c}~$ increase also. By Lemma~\ref{z:l:1} the mean value  increases.
\end{proof}

\medskip
   
    \noindent
     {\bf We finish now the proof of  Step 1:}  For a given level~$\alpha$ let us consider the two rejection regions~$ R_{a,b,c}$ and~$R_{a,b,(c+1)}~$  of the two considered tests in the plane~$F_b,F_c$ and set
     \[
     A:=R_{a,b,c} \setminus R_{a,b,(c+1)} \text{ and } B:= R_{a,b,(c+1)}\setminus R_{a,b,c}\,,
     \] 
     see Figure \ref{fig:power}.  These two regions have  the same~$\nu_0$ measure. By elementary geometry there exist a point~$K=(K_b,K_c)$  in the plane such that 
      \begin{itemize}
      \item For every point of~$A$,~$F_b \leq K_b$,~$F_c \leq  K_c$,
      \item For every point of~$B$,~$F_b \geq K_b$,~$F_c \geq  K_c$,
\end{itemize}
      By transport of measure there exists a transport function~$\mathcal{T}$  that  preserve the measure~$\nu_0$  and  that is one-to one~$A \to B$.   As a consequence  the transport  by~$\mathcal{T}$ improve the probability under the alternative: the power of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c+1}$ is~larger than that of 
     ~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$.  \bigskip

  
  
 \noindent
 {$\circ$ \bf Step 2: } We prove that, when the considered  indexes belong to~$\mathcal I$ such that~$a<b-1$,~$\mathcal{S}_{a,(b-1),c}$ is more powerful than~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$. 
 Our proof is conditional on~$F_a=f_a,F_b =f_b~$ and is located  
 in the plane~$(F_{b-1}, F_c)$. 
 
 
 
 \noindent
  The rejection region~$R_{a,b,c}$ takes the form 
~$F_c \leq  \frac{1}{1-z_1}f_b  -\frac{z_1}{1-z_1}f_a~$
   for some threshold~$z_1$ belonging to~$(0,1)$.\newline
The rejection region~$R_{a,(b-1),c}$ takes the form~$F_c \leq \frac{1}{1-z_2} F_{b-1} - \frac{z_2}{1-z_2} f_a~$ for some  other threshold~$z_2$ belonging to~$(0,1)$. \newline
These regions as well as the regions~$A$ and~$B$ and the point~$K$  are indicated in Figure \ref{fig:power}.

Transport of measure  and the convenient modification of Lemma \ref{jma:lemma} imply that the power of the test $\mathcal{S}_{a,(b-1),c}$ is greater of equal than that of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$.  \bigskip

  Our proof is conditional on~$F_a=f_a,F_{c} =f_{c}~$ and is located in the plane~$F_{a+1}, F_b$.\newline
The rejection region~$R_{a,b,c}$ takes the form~$F_b \geq z_1 f_a + (1-z_1)f_c~$ for some threshold~$z_1$belonging to~$(0,1)$. \newline

Considering the three cases above,  we get the desired result.

nodes.name: Admissible indexes
nodes.statement_short: Set of admissible index triples.
nodes.statement:
Let~$\mathcal I$ the set of admissible indexes 
~$$
 \mathcal I := \{a,b,c: a_0\leq a<b<c \leq K+1 \}\,.
~$$

nodes.name: Step 1
nodes.statement_short: Increasing $c$ increases power.
nodes.statement:
{$\circ$ \bf Step 1: } We prove that, when the considered  indexes such that~$c+1\leq K+1$ belong to~$\mathcal I$,~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c+1}$ is more powerful than~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$. Our proof is conditional to~$F_a=f_a,F_{c+1} =f_{c+1}~$.  Note that~$(F_{a+1}, \ldots, F_c)~$ has for distribution the uniform distribution  on the simplex
~$$
  \mathcal S := \{ f_a>F_{a+1} > \cdots > F_c >f_{c+1} \}.
~$$ 
  This implies  by direct calculations that 
~$$
  \mathcal{I}_{ab}(s,t) =\frac{ (s-t) ^{b-a-1}}{(b-a-1)!}
~$$
  and that 
\begin{equation} \frac{   \mathds{F}_{abc}(\lambda_b)   }{\mathds{F}_{abc}(\lambda_a)} = \boldsymbol{F}_{\beta((b-a),(c-b))} \bigg( \frac{ F_b-F_c}{ f_a-F_c} \bigg).
\end{equation}
  where~$\boldsymbol{F}_\beta$ is the cumulative distribution  of the Beta distribution in reference.  Using monotony of this  function the~$\mathcal{S}_{abc}$ test has for rejection region 
  \begin{equation} (F_b-F_c)  \geq z_1 (f_a-F_c) \Leftrightarrow  F_b \geq z_1 f_a +(1-z_1) F_c,
 \end{equation}
  where~$z_1$ is some threshold, depending on~$\alpha$, that belongs to~$(0,1)$. 
  
  
  Similarly~$\mathcal{S}_{ab(c+1)}$ has for rejection region 
  \begin{equation} F_b \geq z_2 (f_a-f_{c+1})  + f_{c+1},
  \end{equation}
  where~$z_2$ is some other threshold belonging to~$(0,1)$. We use the following lemmas.  
 
 \begin{lemma} Let~$c \leq K$.  The density~$h_\mu$ of~$f_1, \ldots, f_c$, conditional on~$F_{c+1}$ with respect of the Lebesgue measure  under the alternative is  coordinate-wise  non-decreasing and given by~\eqref{zazcosh}.
  \end{lemma}
  \begin{proof}
Observe that it suffises to prove the result when~$\sigma=1$. Note that 
~$$
 \lambda_{c+1}^{i_1, \dots, i_c } =   \max_{j\in[p]\,,\   j\neq \overline \imath_1,\ldots,   j \neq  \overline \imath_c}  |Z_j|.
~$$
  Thus its density~$ p_{\mu^0,i_1,\ldots,i_c}$ does not depend  on~$\mu^0_{ \overline i_1},\ldots,\mu^0_{ \overline i_c}$. As a consequence the following variables have the same distribution ;
$ \lambda_{c+1}^{i_1 +\epsilon_1 p, \dots, i_c +\epsilon_c p}~$ , where~$\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_c$ take the value 0 or 1 and  indices are taken modulo~$p$. 



Because of the independence of the different variables, the joint density, under the alternative hypothesis, of $\lambda_1, \ldots,  \lambda_{c+1}$ taken at~$ \ell_1, \ldots, \ell_{c+1},$  on the domain~$ \{\lambda_1>\cdots > \lambda_{c+1}\}$ takes the value
~$$
 (Const)   \sum'   \big(\varphi(\ell_1 -\mu^0_{j_1} ) +\varphi(\ell_1 +\mu^0_{j_1} ) \big),\ldots ,
   \big(\varphi(\ell_c -\mu^0_{j_c} ) +\varphi(\ell_c +\mu^0_{j_c} ) \big)
  p_{\mu^0,j_1,\ldots,j_K}(\ell_{k+1}).
~$$
Here the sum~$ \displaystyle \sum'$ is taken over all different~$j_1, \ldots, j_c$ belonging  to~$\llbracket 1, p\rrbracket$.
 
 Then the density, conditional on~$F_{c+1} = f_{c+1}$,   of
~$ F_1 ,\ldots,F_{c}~$  at~$f_1,\ldots,f_c$  takes the value
~
\begin{equation} \mathrm{(const)}  \sum'  \cosh( \mu_{j_1} f_1)\ldots \cosh( \mu_{j_c} f_c) \mathds{1}_{f_1>\cdots> f_{c}> F_{c+1}},
\end{equation}
 implying  that this density is coordinate-wise  non-decreasing. 
 \end{proof}
 
 \begin{lemma} Let~$\nu_0$  the image  on the plane~$(F_b,F_c)$  on the uniform probability  on~$\mathcal S$: it is the distribution  under the null of~$(F_b,F_c)$. The two rejection regions :~$\mathcal R_1$ associated to 
\eqref{ZAZA:e:r1} and~$\mathcal R_2$ associated to 
\eqref{ZAZA:e:r2} 
have  of course the same probability~$\alpha$ under~$\nu_0$. Let~$\eta_{\mu^0}$ the density w.r.t.~$\nu_0$ of the distribution of~$(F_b,F_c)$ under the alternative. Then~$\eta_{\mu^0}$     is non decreasing coordinate-wise. 
  \end{lemma}
  \begin{proof}  
Integration yields that density of~$\nu_0$ w.r.t. the Lebesgue    measure taken at point~$(f_b,f_c)$  is 
\[
 \frac{  (f_a-f_b)^{b-a-1}   (f_b-f_c)^{c-b-1}  }{(b-a-1)!(c-b-1)!}.
\]
  The density of~$\nu_{\mu^0}$  w.r.t. Lebesgue measure  is 
  \begin{equation} \int _{f_b} ^{f_a} df_{a+1} \ldots   \int _{f_b} ^{f_b-2} df_{a+1}  \int _{f_b} ^{f_b-2} df_{b-1} 
   \int _{f_c} ^{f_b} df_{b+1} \ldots   \int _{f_c} ^{f_{c-2}} df_{c-1}   h_{\mu^0}(f_{a},\ldots ,f_c).
 \end{equation}
  Thus~$\eta_{\mu^0}$ which is the quotient  of these two quantities is just  a mean value  of~$h_{\mu^0}$ on the domain  of integration~$\mathcal D_{f_b,f_c}$  in~\eqref{ZAZA:e:vm}.
  
  Suppose that~$f_b$ and~$ f_c$  increase, then all the borns of the domain~$\mathcal D_{f_b,f_c}~$ increase also. By Lemma~\ref{z:l:1} the mean value  increases.
\end{proof}

\medskip
   
    \noindent
     {\bf We finish now the proof of  Step 1:}  For a given level~$\alpha$ let us consider the two rejection regions~$ R_{a,b,c}$ and~$R_{a,b,(c+1)}~$  of the two considered tests in the plane~$F_b,F_c$ and set
     \[
     A:=R_{a,b,c} \setminus R_{a,b,(c+1)} \text{ and } B:= R_{a,b,(c+1)}\setminus R_{a,b,c}\,,
     \] 
     see Figure \ref{fig:power}.  These two regions have  the same~$\nu_0$ measure. By elementary geometry there exist a point~$K=(K_b,K_c)$  in the plane such that 
      \begin{itemize}
      \item For every point of~$A$,~$F_b \leq K_b$,~$F_c \leq  K_c$,
      \item For every point of~$B$,~$F_b \geq K_b$,~$F_c \geq  K_c$,
\end{itemize}
      By transport of measure there exists a transport function~$\mathcal{T}$  that  preserve the measure~$\nu_0$  and  that is one-to one~$A \to B$.   As a consequence  the transport  by~$\mathcal{T}$ improve the probability under the alternative: the power of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c+1}$ is~larger than that of 
     ~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$.

   \int _{f_c} ^{f_b} df_{b+1} \ldots   \int _{f_c} ^{f_{c-2}} df_{c-1}   h_{\mu^0}(f_{a},\ldots ,f_c).

nodes.name: Monotonicity
nodes.statement_short: Monotone bounds and monotone density give monotone ratio.
nodes.statement: Suppose that~$f_b$ and~$ f_c$  increase, then all the borns of the domain~$\mathcal D_{f_b,f_c}~$ increase also. By Lemma~\ref{z:l:1} the mean value  increases.

nodes.name: Finish Step 1
nodes.statement_short: Measure-preserving transport from $A$ to $B$ increases alternative probability.
nodes.statement:
{\bf We finish now the proof of  Step 1:}  For a given level~$\alpha$ let us consider the two rejection regions~$ R_{a,b,c}$ and~$R_{a,b,(c+1)}~$  of the two considered tests in the plane~$F_b,F_c$ and set
     \[
     A:=R_{a,b,c} \setminus R_{a,b,(c+1)} \text{ and } B:= R_{a,b,(c+1)}\setminus R_{a,b,c}\,,
     \] 
     see Figure \ref{fig:power}.  These two regions have  the same~$\nu_0$ measure. By elementary geometry there exist a point~$K=(K_b,K_c)$  in the plane such that 
      \begin{itemize}
      \item For every point of~$A$,~$F_b \leq K_b$,~$F_c \leq  K_c$,
      \item For every point of~$B$,~$F_b \geq K_b$,~$F_c \geq  K_c$,
\end{itemize}
      By transport of measure there exists a transport function~$\mathcal{T}$  that  preserve the measure~$\nu_0$  and  that is one-to one~$A \to B$.   As a consequence  the transport  by~$\mathcal{T}$ improve the probability under the alternative: the power of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c+1}$ is~larger than that of 
     ~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$.

nodes.name: Regions A and B
nodes.statement_short: Regions $A$ and $B$ have equal null measure.
nodes.statement:
For a given level~$\alpha$ let us consider the two rejection regions~$ R_{a,b,c}$ and~$R_{a,b,(c+1)}~$  of the two considered tests in the plane~$F_b,F_c$ and set
     \[
     A:=R_{a,b,c} \setminus R_{a,b,(c+1)} \text{ and } B:= R_{a,b,(c+1)}\setminus R_{a,b,c}\,,
     \] 
     see Figure \ref{fig:power}.  These two regions have  the same~$\nu_0$ measure.

nodes.name: Separating point
nodes.statement_short: A point $K$ separates $A$ (below-left) from $B$ (above-right).

nodes.name: Points of A
nodes.statement_short: Points of $A$ lie below-left of $K$.
nodes.statement: For every point of~$A$,~$F_b \leq K_b$,~$F_c \leq  K_c$,

nodes.name: Points of B
nodes.statement_short: Points of $B$ lie above-right of $K$.
nodes.statement: For every point of~$B$,~$F_b \geq K_b$,~$F_c \geq  K_c$,

nodes.name: Transport
nodes.statement_short: A measure-preserving map $A\to B$ increases the alternative probability.
nodes.statement:
By transport of measure there exists a transport function~$\mathcal{T}$  that  preserve the measure~$\nu_0$  and  that is one-to one~$A \to B$.   As a consequence  the transport  by~$\mathcal{T}$ improve the probability under the alternative: the power of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c+1}$ is~larger than that of 
     ~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$.

nodes.name: Step 2
nodes.statement_short: Decreasing $b$ increases power.
nodes.statement:
{$\circ$ \bf Step 2: } We prove that, when the considered  indexes belong to~$\mathcal I$ such that~$a<b-1$,~$\mathcal{S}_{a,(b-1),c}$ is more powerful than~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$. 
 Our proof is conditional on~$F_a=f_a,F_b =f_b~$ and is located  
 in the plane~$(F_{b-1}, F_c)$. 
 
 
 
 \noindent
  The rejection region~$R_{a,b,c}$ takes the form 
~$F_c \leq  \frac{1}{1-z_1}f_b  -\frac{z_1}{1-z_1}f_a~$
   for some threshold~$z_1$ belonging to~$(0,1)$.\newline
The rejection region~$R_{a,(b-1),c}$ takes the form~$F_c \leq \frac{1}{1-z_2} F_{b-1} - \frac{z_2}{1-z_2} f_a~$ for some  other threshold~$z_2$ belonging to~$(0,1)$. \newline
These regions as well as the regions~$A$ and~$B$ and the point~$K$  are indicated in Figure \ref{fig:power}.

Transport of measure  and the convenient modification of Lemma \ref{jma:lemma} imply that the power of the test $\mathcal{S}_{a,(b-1),c}$ is greater of equal than that of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$.

nodes.name: Conditioning
nodes.statement_short: Condition on $F_a$, $F_b$.
nodes.statement:
We prove that, when the considered  indexes belong to~$\mathcal I$ such that~$a<b-1$,~$\mathcal{S}_{a,(b-1),c}$ is more powerful than~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$. 
 Our proof is conditional on~$F_a=f_a,F_b =f_b~$ and is located  
 in the plane~$(F_{b-1}, F_c)$.

nodes.statement_short: Linear rejection regions.

~$F_c \leq  \frac{1}{1-z_1}f_b  -\frac{z_1}{1-z_1}f_a~$
   for some threshold~$z_1$ belonging to~$(0,1)$.\newline
The rejection region~$R_{a,(b-1),c}$ takes the form~$F_c \leq \frac{1}{1-z_2} F_{b-1} - \frac{z_2}{1-z_2} f_a~$ for some  other threshold~$z_2$ belonging to~$(0,1)$. \newline
These regions as well as the regions~$A$ and~$B$ and the point~$K$  are indicated in Figure \ref{fig:power}.

nodes.name: Conclude Step 2
nodes.statement_short: Transport argument as in Step 1.
nodes.statement: Transport of measure  and the convenient modification of Lemma \ref{jma:lemma} imply that the power of the test $\mathcal{S}_{a,(b-1),c}$ is greater of equal than that of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$.

nodes.name: Step 3
nodes.statement_short: Decreasing $a$ increases power.
nodes.statement:
{$\circ$ \bf Step 3: } We prove that, when the considered  indexes belong to~$\mathcal I$ such that~$a+1<b$,~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$ is more powerful than~$\mathcal{S}_{(a+1),b,c}$. 
  Our proof is conditional on~$F_a=f_a,F_{c} =f_{c}~$ and is located in the plane~$F_{a+1}, F_b$.\newline
The rejection region~$R_{a,b,c}$ takes the form~$F_b \geq z_1 f_a + (1-z_1)f_c~$ for some threshold~$z_1$belonging to~$(0,1)$. \newline
 The rejection region~$R_{a+1,b,c}$ takes the form~$F_b \geq z_2 F_{a+1} + (1-z_2)f_c ~$ for some  other threshold~$z_2$ belonging to~$(0,1)$.\newline
These regions as well as the regions~$A$ and~$B$ and the point~$K$  are indicated in Figure \ref{fig:power}.

Transport of measure  and  the convenient modification of Lemma \ref{jma:lemma} imply that the power of~$\mathcal{S}_{a,b,c}$ is greater of equal  that that of~$\mathcal{S}_{(a+1),b,c}$.

nodes.name: Proof of the residual simplification lemma
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$ using the residual recursion and the three-perpendicular identity for $\theta$ and $\Pi$.
nodes.statement:
The proof works by induction. Let us check the relation for~$k=2$, namely
\[
 N^{(1)} -\lambda_{1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1)=Z-Z_{\widehat \imath_1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1)=Z - \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1}  (Z)\,.
\]
Now, let~$k\geq 3$. First, the three perpendicular theorem  implies  that  for every~$j,  i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}~$,
\begin{align*}
	\theta_j(i_1, \ldots ,  i_{k-2})
   	&= \big(R_{j,i_1} \cdots R_{j,i_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}}   
		( 
 			\theta_{i_1}(i_1, \ldots ,  i_{k-2}),\ldots,\theta_{i_{k-1}} (i_1,\ldots, i_{k-2})  
  		)\,,\\
	\mathrm{and}\ \Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-2}}  (Z_j)
	&= \big(R_{j,i_1} \cdots R_{j,i_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}}   
		( 
  			\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-2}}  (Z_{i_1}),\ldots,\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-2}}  (Z_{i_{k-1}})  
  		)\,.
\end{align*}
By induction, using~\eqref{eq:value_nk}, we get that
\begin{align}
N^{(k-1)}&=N^{(k-2)}-(\lambda_{k-2}-\lambda_{k-1}) \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,,\notag
\\
&=
(N^{(k-2)}-\lambda_{k-2} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2}))+\lambda_{k-1}\theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,,\notag\\
&=
Z  - \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-2}}  (Z)+\lambda_{k-1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,. \end{align}
Then, recall that~$N^{(k-1)}_j = \lambda_{k-1}$ for~$j=\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}$ and remark that
\[
\lambda_{k-1} \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}) 
= \big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}} 
 (N^{(k-1)}_{\widehat \imath_1},\ldots,N^{(k-1)}_{\widehat \imath_{k-1}})\,.
\]
Using~\eqref{eq:induc} at indices~$j=\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}$, we deduce that
\begin{align*}
\lambda_{k-1} \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1,&\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}) \\
&
= \big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}} 
 (N^{(k-1)}_{\widehat \imath_1},\ldots,N^{(k-1)}_{\widehat \imath_{k-1}})
\\
& = \big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}} 
   (Z_{\widehat \imath_1},\ldots,Z_{\widehat \imath_{k-1}})
\\
 &\quad - \big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}}   
	( 
  		\Pi_{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots,\widehat\imath_{k-2}}  (Z_{\widehat \imath_1}),\ldots,\Pi_{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2}}  (Z_{\widehat \imath_{k-1}})  
  	)
\\
&\quad + \lambda_{k-1}\big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}}   
( 
 \theta_{\widehat \imath_1}(\,\widehat \imath_1, \ldots , \widehat\imath_{k-2}),\ldots,\theta_{\widehat \imath_{k-1}} (\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat\imath_{k-2})  
  ) 
\\
& = \Pi_{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots,\widehat\imath_{k-1}}  (Z_{j})- \Pi_{\widehat\imath_1,\ldots,\widehat\imath_{k-2}}  (Z_j)
+\lambda_{k-1} \theta_j(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-2}) \,,
  \end{align*}
  Namely
  \[
  \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  (Z)-\lambda_{k-1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1})
  =
  \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-2}}  (Z)-\lambda_{k-1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,.
  \]
Using again~\eqref{eq:induc} we get that
\begin{align*}
 N^{(k-1)}&= Z  - \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-2}}  (Z)+\lambda_{k-1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-2})\,,\\
 &=Z  - \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  (Z)+\lambda_{k-1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1})\,,
\end{align*}
as claimed.

nodes.statement_short: Base case $k=2$.
nodes.statement:
The proof works by induction. Let us check the relation for~$k=2$, namely

 N^{(1)} -\lambda_{1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1)=Z-Z_{\widehat \imath_1} \theta(\,\widehat \imath_1)=Z - \Pi_{\widehat \imath_1}  (Z)\,.
\]

Then, recall that~$N^{(k-1)}_j = \lambda_{k-1}$ for~$j=\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}$ and remark that

\]
Using~\eqref{eq:induc} at indices~$j=\widehat \imath_1,\ldots,\widehat \imath_{k-1}$, we deduce that

\\
& = \big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}}

\\
 &\quad - \big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}}   
	(

  	)

&\quad + \lambda_{k-1}\big(R_{j,\widehat \imath_1} \cdots R_{j,\widehat \imath_{k-1}}  \big)M^{-1}_{\widehat \imath_1,\ldots, \widehat \imath_{k-1}}

nodes.name: Proof of the recursion for the frozen residuals
nodes.statement_short: Schur complement and LU block inversion show numerators and denominators of the two expressions coincide.
nodes.statement:
We denote
\begin{align*}
R_{j}&:=\big(R_{j, i_1}, \ldots, R_{j,i_{k-1}}  \big)\,,\\
R_{i_k}&:=\big(R_{i_k, i_1} ,\ldots ,R_{ i_k, i_{k-1}} \big)\,,\\
M&:=M_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}}\,,\\
\overline M&:=M_{i_1,\ldots, i_{k}}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}M & R_{i_k} \\R_{i_k}^\top & R_{i_k,i_k}\end{array}\right]\,,\\
\overline R&:=\big(R_{j, i_1}, \ldots, R_{j,i_{k}}  \big)\,,\\

x&:=\frac{1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}{1-\theta_{i_k}(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}\frac{\tau_{j,i_k}}{\tau_{i_k,i_k}}\,,
\end{align*}
and observe that
\begin{align}
x&=\frac
{R_{j,i_k} -R_j^\top M^{-1}R_{i_k}}
{R_{i_k,i_k} -R_{i_k}^\top M^{-1}R_{i_k}}\,,\notag\\
{\overline M}^{-1}&=
\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{Id}_{k-1} & -M^{-1}R_{i_k} \\0 & 1\end{array}\right]
\left[\begin{array}{cc}M^{-1} & 0 \\0 & \big(R_{i_k,i_k} -R_{i_k}^\top M^{-1}R_{i_k}\big)^{-1}\end{array}\right]
\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{Id}_{k-1} & 0 \\-R_{i_k}^{\top}M^{-1} & 1\end{array}\right]\,,\notag\\
{\overline M}^{-1}\overline R&=
\left[\begin{array}{c}M^{-1}\big(R_j-xR_{i_k}\big) \\ x\end{array}\right]\,, \end{align}
using Schur complement of block~$M$ of the matrix~$\overline M$ and a LU decomposition. Note also that
\[
\frac{Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_j-Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})}_{i_k}\tau_{j,i_k}/\tau_{i_k,i_k}}
{1-\tau_{j,i_k}/\tau_{i_k,i_k}}
=\frac
{Z_j-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z_j)-x\,(Z_{i_k}-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z_{i_k}))}
{1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})-x(1-\theta_{i_k}(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}))}\,.
\]
To prove~\eqref{eq:rec_Zj}, it suffices to show that the R.H.S term  above is equal to the following R.H.S term
\[
Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j=
\frac{Z_j-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k}} (Z_j)}
{1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}\,.
\]
We will prove that numerators are equal and that denominators are equal. For denominators, 
\begin{align}
&1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})-x(1-\theta_{i_k}(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}))\notag\\
&=1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})-x+x\,\theta_{i_k}(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})\notag\\
&=1-(\underbrace{1\cdots 1}_{k\ \mathrm{times}})
\left[\begin{array}{c}M^{-1}\big(R_j-xR_{i_k}\big) \\ x\end{array}\right]\notag\\
&=1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k}) \,,
\end{align}
using~\eqref{eq:Schur1}. Furthermore, it proves~\eqref{eq:sign_tau}. For the numerators, we use that
\begin{align*}
&Z_j-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z_j)-x\,(Z_{i_k}-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z_{i_k}))\\
&=Z_j-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z_j)-x Z_{i_k}+ x \Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}} (Z_{i_k})\\
&=Z_j-(Z_{i_1}\cdots Z_{i_k})
\left[\begin{array}{c}M^{-1}\big(R_j-xR_{i_k}\big) \\ x\end{array}\right]\\
&=Z_j-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k}} (Z_j)\,.
\end{align*}
using~\eqref{eq:Schur1}.

nodes.name: Schur complement
nodes.statement_short: Notation and block inverse via Schur complement.
nodes.statement:
We denote
\begin{align*}
R_{j}&:=\big(R_{j, i_1}, \ldots, R_{j,i_{k-1}}  \big)\,,\\
R_{i_k}&:=\big(R_{i_k, i_1} ,\ldots ,R_{ i_k, i_{k-1}} \big)\,,\\

\begin{align}
x&=\frac
{R_{j,i_k} -R_j^\top M^{-1}R_{i_k}}
{R_{i_k,i_k} -R_{i_k}^\top M^{-1}R_{i_k}}\,,\notag\\
{\overline M}^{-1}&=
\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{Id}_{k-1} & -M^{-1}R_{i_k} \\0 & 1\end{array}\right]
\left[\begin{array}{cc}M^{-1} & 0 \\0 & \big(R_{i_k,i_k} -R_{i_k}^\top M^{-1}R_{i_k}\big)^{-1}\end{array}\right]
\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{Id}_{k-1} & 0 \\-R_{i_k}^{\top}M^{-1} & 1\end{array}\right]\,,\notag\\
{\overline M}^{-1}\overline R&=
\left[\begin{array}{c}M^{-1}\big(R_j-xR_{i_k}\big) \\ x\end{array}\right]\,, \end{align}
using Schur complement of block~$M$ of the matrix~$\overline M$ and a LU decomposition.

nodes.name: Equation (7.9)
nodes.statement:

{R_{j,i_k} -R_j^\top M^{-1}R_{i_k}}
{R_{i_k,i_k} -R_{i_k}^\top M^{-1}R_{i_k}}\,,\notag\\
{\overline M}^{-1}&=
\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{Id}_{k-1} & -M^{-1}R_{i_k} \\0 & 1\end{array}\right]
\left[\begin{array}{cc}M^{-1} & 0 \\0 & \big(R_{i_k,i_k} -R_{i_k}^\top M^{-1}R_{i_k}\big)^{-1}\end{array}\right]
\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{Id}_{k-1} & 0 \\-R_{i_k}^{\top}M^{-1} & 1\end{array}\right]\,,\notag\\

nodes.label: eq:Schur1

nodes.name: Rewrite
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the recursion's right-hand side.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to equality of numerators and denominators.
nodes.statement:
To prove~\eqref{eq:rec_Zj}, it suffices to show that the R.H.S term  above is equal to the following R.H.S term
\[
Z^{(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}_j=
\frac{Z_j-\Pi_{ i_1,\ldots, i_{k}} (Z_j)}
{1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k})}\,.
\]

nodes.name: Denominators
nodes.statement_short: Denominators agree; this also gives the ratio identity.
nodes.statement:
We will prove that numerators are equal and that denominators are equal. For denominators, 
\begin{align}
&1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})-x(1-\theta_{i_k}(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1}))\notag\\
&=1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})-x+x\,\theta_{i_k}(i_1,\ldots, i_{k-1})\notag\\
&=1-(\underbrace{1\cdots 1}_{k\ \mathrm{times}})
\left[\begin{array}{c}M^{-1}\big(R_j-xR_{i_k}\big) \\ x\end{array}\right]\notag\\
&=1-\theta_j(i_1,\ldots, i_{k}) \,,
\end{align}
using~\eqref{eq:Schur1}. Furthermore, it proves~\eqref{eq:sign_tau}.
